Bootstrap multiple linear regression for stroke prediction

Sebastian Ross

2026-09-12

url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Kingsoul42/STA-321/main/dataset/healthcare-dataset-stroke-data.csv"

stroke_predictions <- read.csv(url, header = TRUE)

1 Introduction

We are going to look at a data set that has many factors to predict if people will have a stroke based on various factors. According to the World Health Organization that strokes are the second leading cause of death with approximtly 11% of totals death. We would like to produce who could have a stroke to try and help save lives. This data set comes from https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fedesoriano/stroke-prediction-dataset. id: number to identify each person gender: gender of each person age: age of the person hypertension: denotes if the person has hyoertension heart_disease: denotes if a person has heart disease ever_married: denotes if a person has been married work_type: denotes what type of workplace they are a part of Residence_type: denotes what types they use avg_glucose_level: denotes their avrage glucose level in their blood bmi: denotes their bmi smoking_status: denotes if they smoke have ever smoked or have never smoked stroke: if the person has ever had a stroke

We are trying to find the association of these factors and how they affect the likelihood of a stroke.

2 Exploritory Data Analysis

We are going to look at the categorical predictor variables to look for any categories that are over and under represented in these studies through bar graphs.

df <- stroke_predictions[, c("gender","hypertension","heart_disease","ever_married","work_type","Residence_type","smoking_status","stroke")]
ggplot(df, aes(x = gender)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Gender distribution Figure 1", x = "Gender", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(hypertension))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Hypertension distribution Figure 2", x = "Hypertension (0 = No, 1 = Yes)", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(heart_disease))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Heart Disease distribution Figure 3", x = "Heart Disease (0 = No, 1 = Yes)", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = ever_married)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Ever Married distribution Figure 4", x = "Ever Married", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = work_type)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Work Type distribution Figure 5", x = "Work Type", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = Residence_type)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Residence Type distribution Figure 6", x = "Residence Type", y = "Count")

ggplot(df, aes(x = smoking_status)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Smoking Status distribution Figure 7", x = "Smoking Status", y = "Count")

As we can see in figure 1 we have a relatively even distribution for male and female but we only have 1 representative of the other classification.We also see in figure 6 that there is a relatively even distribution in rural and urban residences in this study. Where figure 4 is also well represented in both groups but having more in the married classification. There are still more women in this study but it is not as far off compared to other groupings. Where in figure 2, 3 ,and 5 we see a big disparity in the groupings on those figure with Never_worked being the least represented in these figures. Where we see in figure 7 there is a close number of former smokers and smokers but there is a big gap between the never smoked and the unknown where we could not get the information on their smoking status. Though these the only group that is to small for us to do much with is the other classification with 1 observation where every other category is represented enough with Never_worked being the second closest to not being represented enough. We also see that id is a predictor variable but it is not helpful in this situation as it is just a way to tell each person apart from each other. We also Imputed the missing values in the bmi using the mice library so they all have values for our linear regression.

3 Model building

Now we will try and build a model using a couple of different methods backwards and forward step wise functions.

predictors <- c("age", "hypertension", "heart_disease", "stroke",
                "bmi", "gender", "ever_married", "work_type",
                "Residence_type", "smoking_status")

full_model <- lm(
  avg_glucose_level ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease + stroke +
           bmi + gender + ever_married + work_type +
           Residence_type + smoking_status,
  data = stroke_predictions_imp,
)
summary(full_model)

4 Model diognostics

par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(full_model)

In the top left we see that the variance is not constant and worse at predicting higher values for glucose levels. Then for top right we see that this model makes extreme predictions both on the high and the low end. Now for the bottom left we see that the variance grows as the predicted values go up. Now for the bottom right we see no high leverage points but the grouping shows that it has some problems in those cases

par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(forward_step)

We see a lot of the same issues from the full model which makes sense given the models are really close with smoking status and residence status are the only things removed between these models.

5 Transformations

We will now do a bos cox transformation on the previous models to try and fix some of the issues with the model assumptions.

boxcox(full_model, lambda = seq(-1.25, -.5, 1/5))

stroke_predictions_imp$glucose_bc <- (stroke_predictions_imp$avg_glucose_level^(-0.9) - 1) / (-0.9)
full_model_bc <- lm(
  glucose_bc ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease + stroke+
               bmi + gender + ever_married + work_type +
               Residence_type + smoking_status,
  data = stroke_predictions_imp
)

-.9 and -1 would be good lamda values for and we will look at model diagnosis for the the box cox transformation

par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(full_model_bc)

The residuals of the full model with the box cox transformation are about the same with still non constant variance and a distinct pattern still present. This makes it so we should still look into using a non parametric test like the bootstraps

par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(backward_bc)

The same goes form the same for the reduced model it looks roughly the same just like the full model and the pre-transformed model. showing that we should use a non-parametric test like the bootstraps method.

6 Residuals of Transformation

select=function(m){ # m is an object: model
 e = m$resid                           # residuals
 n0 = length(e)                        # sample size
 SSE=(m$df)*(summary(m)$sigma)^2       # sum of squared error
 R.sq=summary(m)$r.squared             # Coefficient of determination: R square!
 R.adj=summary(m)$adj.r                # Adjusted R square
 MSE=(summary(m)$sigma)^2              # square error
 Cp=(SSE/MSE)-(n0-2*(n0-m$df))         # Mellow's p
 AIC=n0*log(SSE)-n0*log(n0)+2*(n0-m$df)          # Akaike information criterion
 SBC=n0*log(SSE)-n0*log(n0)+(log(n0))*(n0-m$df)  # Schwarz Bayesian Information criterion
 X=model.matrix(m)                     # design matrix of the model
 H=X%*%solve(t(X)%*%X)%*%t(X)          # hat matrix
 d=e/(1-diag(H))                       
 PRESS=t(d)%*%d   # predicted residual error sum of squares (PRESS)- a cross-validation measure
 tbl = as.data.frame(cbind(SSE=SSE, R.sq=R.sq, R.adj = R.adj, Cp = Cp, AIC = AIC, SBC = SBC, PRD = PRESS))
 names(tbl)=c("SSE", "R.sq", "R.adj", "Cp", "AIC", "SBC", "PRESS")
 tbl
 }
output.sum = rbind(select(full_model), select(full_model_bc), select(backward_bc))
row.names(output.sum) = c("full_model", "full_model transform", "reduced transformed")
kable(output.sum, caption = "Goodness-of-fit Measures of Candidate Models")
Goodness-of-fit Measures of Candidate Models
SSE R.sq R.adj Cp AIC SBC PRESS
full_model 9.419961e+06 0.1008501 0.0980254 17 38458.07 38569.23 1.010336e+07

reduced transformed 1.378018e-01 0.0580447 0.0558270 13 -53735.77 -53650.76 1.386318e-01

Based on the table the two transformed models are stronger than the original full model. But the differences between the two transformed models are not that different even with the transformed full model is stronger it is not by much. So I would use the transformed reduced model for the less dimentinality and making it slightly easier to understand.

7 Final model

We will be looking at the final model that is easier to understand which is the transformed reduced model.

We see that from these that most of the variables are significant the only ones that aren’t are different levels of different variables. which are necessary for out analysis of the other categories. 1.0896+ 0.0000331* age+ 0.00134* hypertension+ 0.00173* heart_disease+ 0.00120* Stroke +0.0000682* bmi+ 0.000426* genderMale+ 0.00765* genderOther+ 0.000176* ever_marriedYes− 0.00149* work_typeGovt_job −0.000516* work_typeNever_worked− 0.00128* work_typePrivate −0.00155* work_typeSelf‑employed Important to note that these are transformed with \(\lambda\)=.9 making it harder to interpret. with \[Y^{*} \;=\; \frac{Y^{-0.9} - 1}{-0.9} \;=\frac{1 - Y^{-0.9}}{0.9}\] this is how we get to the point where we get the values from

8 Discussions

With this we can see that a increases you average glucose level by .000331 hypertension raises it by .00134 for heart disease raised by .00173 for stroke by .0012 bmi raises by .00426 and male by .00765 and other by .00765 and finally it is raied by .000176 for ever_marriedYes. Where they are lowered by .00149 for work_typeGovt_job lowered by .000516 for work_typeNever_worked lowered by 0.00128 for work_typePrivate and finally lowered by 0.00155 for work_typeSelf‑employed. Age, bmi, stroke, hypertension, and heart disease are the strongest predictors. We need to to keep some of the never work with the others being significant and we can’t get rid of the factor level just because it is not significant. gender other is the same but it is hard to tell how impact that level is with there only being one observation of other. being male also seems to raise your average glucose level compareded to the other genders. while being married is important as a factor level for never married. We see that the box cox transformation didn’t do that much in fixing the issues of the model assumptions. This makes these p-values hard to determine how useful these P values are with some of the model assumptions being broken. This shows we need to look at using a non-parametric test such as the bootstraps.
